# Mine

A set of small PWAs that keep your personal data as markdown in a private GitHub repo —
calendar, zettelkasten, diary — so it stays portable and free of vendor lock-in.

**Live: https://maximilianharr.github.io/mine/** — install it to your home screen.

## Docs

| | |
| --- | --- |
| [REQUIREMENTS.md](REQUIREMENTS.md) | what the app does and how it behaves |
| [TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md](TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md) | how it is built, and the verified platform findings |
| [TEST-REQUIREMENTS.md](TEST-REQUIREMENTS.md) | what is checked before a change ships, and how |
| [calendar/](calendar/) | the calendar app, with its own pair of docs |

## Layout

```
index.html app.js style.css sw.js manifest.json   the main app
shared/   apps.js store.js github.js md.js        used by every app
          markdown.js prefs.js vendor/
calendar/                                         one folder per app
spike/                                            on-device platform checks
test/                                             the checks: test/run.sh
```

No build step: no bundler, no CI, no dependencies to install. `git push` deploys to GitHub
Pages. To run it locally, `python3 -m http.server` in this folder and open the printed URL.
`test/run.sh` runs the model checks in node and the rest in a headless browser, and installs
nothing either.

Data lives in a **separate private repo**, never in this one. The token is entered once in the
app, stored on the device, and scoped so it can only touch that data repo.

## Status

The main app, the sync layer and the on-device checks are done and verified end to end against a
real repo. The calendar is built — the five views, the kanban, the entry popup and its field
popups, the settings panel — and `test/run.sh` covers it.

Not built yet: the per-app summary above the tiles that [REQUIREMENTS.md](REQUIREMENTS.md)
describes. The tile screen shows tiles only, so opening the calendar is currently the only way
to see what is on today.

column may show at the edge of the screen: a sliver of `done` beside `doing` is a layout fault,
and the cause is always the same — a gap between columns in a strip that is shifted by whole
column widths. Stacked, all three stages are on screen by design and this says nothing.

Cards are not reordered by hand; their order comes from importance and start — the important ones
first, each block by start date.

## The filter and the settings

**One button opens both.** The hamburger opens a centred panel, titled `Calendar`, whose top
right has an `x` to close, and it holds two sections: **the filter at the top, the settings
below it**, under a heading each.

They are one panel because they are one errand. Both are things you adjust about the view in
front of you and then leave alone, and two buttons a thumb's width apart — one to hide a group,
one to change the week's first day — asked which of the two a given switch was before you could
reach it. Merging them also freed the slot the zoom took, which is what keeps the pane at four
controls and the phone's first row from gaining a fifth.

The filter comes first because it is the half you open often: a group hidden this afternoon, the
board narrowed to what is important. The settings are the nine rows that change once.

| section | holds |
| --- | --- |
| Filter | the groups dropdown; on the board also **important only** and an **assignee** |
| Settings | the nine rows below |

**Groups stay a dropdown inside the filter, not a list**: one `groups` row saying how many are
on, which opens to the same checkboxes, each group showing its colour. Any subset can still be
hidden — the dropdown only folds the list away. Folded is how it starts, and that is now load
bearing twice over: a repo with twenty groups would otherwise give the panel a filter taller
than the screen *and* push the nine settings rows below the fold. This is a view filter and is
remembered per device; groups are *named and coloured* in the settings section's **edit groups**,
not here.

**Every row is two halves: the label in the left half, its control in the right.** That one rule
is what the panel was missing. A select, a text box, a checkbox and a date field each began
wherever its own label happened to end, so nine tidy rows read as a ragged column — and the fix
is alignment, not fewer settings. The controls now line up in one column down the panel.

Nine rows, and the labels are short enough to fit their half on one line at 320 px — which is
why two of them are no longer named after the kanban:

| row | control |
| --- | --- |
| Groups | an **edit groups** button |
| Start week on | Monday or Sunday |
| Time zone | a zone name such as `Europe/Berlin`, defaulting to the device's own |
| Date format | `auto` (the device's locale), `dd.mm.yyyy` or `mm/dd/yy` |
| Calendar weeks | the month view's week-number gutter |
| Confirm discard | whether leaving an edited popup asks before discarding |
| Sprint length | in weeks |
| First sprint | the date sprint 1 starts on |
| Theme | system, light or dark |

Those are labels only: the two renamed rows still read and write `kanban-interval` and
`kanban-anchor` in the repo, because renaming a row must not rewrite a file.

**Groups are behind the button, not listed in the panel.** *Edit groups* opens the category
popup in its manage-only form — every group with its colour, a `+ add`, a pen and a trashcan. A
list in the panel grew with the repo and pushed the nine settings that never change below the
fold, which is the one thing a settings panel must not do.

**The panel ends at its last settings row.** There is no paragraph under it explaining what is
stored where. That rule is the next two paragraphs, and it belongs in this document rather than
on a screen you opened to change the theme.

A zone name, not an offset: a plain `UTC+1` is an hour wrong for half the year in any zone with
daylight saving. This zone, not the device's, decides which day a timed entry lands in, where it
sits in the week and day grids, and what a time you type means. All-day entries are bare dates
and are never run through it at all. The week view's label carries its ISO week number whether
*calendar weeks* is on or off: that row governs the month view's gutter and nothing else.

Everything in either section is stored on the device except the groups, the sprint length and the
first sprint date, which are data and live in the repo so they follow you and mean the same thing
everywhere. The board's orientation is a device preference too, and the one of them with no row
here: it is picked in the zoom, where it is read as a view control rather than as a setting.
Theme and date format apply to all of Mine, not the calendar alone, and the main app's settings
shows the same two rows.

## On a phone

The views above describe the desktop. The same screens adapt:

- The top pane is **two rows**: `[board] [zoom] [☰] [⌂]` sharing the first equally, and
  `[‹] [NOV/26] [›]` filling the second, at twice their old size and at every phone width, 320

- A month cell shows at most two entry lines, then `+N`; a line carries the title alone, with no
  time prefix and no done-rectangle, clipped at the cell's edge. A year cell stays a coloured
  day.

The row and its controls are one place where a click that does two things is easy to build.

**Five of the six fields are rows**, in this canonical order:

- a ball for **category**;
- circular arrows for **repetition**;
- a bell for **alerts**;
- a pin for **location**;
- a person for **participants**.

The sixth, **details**, is not a row: it is the body, and it is drawn in full at the foot of the
popup — described below. A markdown body is the one value that cannot be read on one line, so a
row is the wrong shape for it, and putting it first in the order the way a row would be sorted
pushes everything else below the fold on any entry with an agenda in it. It keeps its place in
the canonical order of fields everywhere that order is a list of fields; it simply is not one of
the rows that order sorts.

**Every editor opens in its own row.** There is no popup over the popup any more: the field
popups are gone, and with them the rule that a sub-popup never writes to the repo — the rows do
not write either, so there is nothing left to carve out. The card scrolls, so a textarea fits in
a row as well as it fitted in a card of its own. The one survivor of that mechanism is the group
manager behind *edit groups*, which is not editing a field.

**Picking a category takes it.** Tapping a group puts it in the draft and closes the row — there
is nothing more to say about a choice from a list, and with no save in the row there is nothing
for a second tap to press. It is the one row that closes itself.

### The title, the when, and the toggle row

**The title is a row too** — text until clicked, then an input with the trio. So is **the when**,
which reads `MON, 20.11.2026 · 09:00–10:00` and opens the start and end date and time inputs
inside the row. Four input boxes at the top of a popup opened to find out what day something is
on was the form at its least readable, and this is the row that had the most to gain.

The when-line no longer repeats the stage, the importance and the estimate as words. The toggle
row shows all three, live, directly beneath it.

### The toggle row

One row of icons directly under the when. These are not fields with an editor each: they are
small values, edited in the row itself with a single tap, and they **show their value** rather
than merely whether they have one — each as a small badge on the corner of its icon.

**A tap on one of them is the whole edit**, into the draft like everything else — there is
nothing in these four to type, so there is nothing for a row's `x` to put back and no editor to
open. The disk appears on the first tap, as it does for any other change.

- **`24h` for all-day** — the one control in the popup that is a word rather than a picture, and
  deliberately so: every drawing of a whole day reads as something else. The sun it replaces was
  taken for weather or for daylight hours, and `24h` cannot be. **A clickable control, not a
  checkbox** — lit when on, plain when off. On an event it is alone on the row. Only the button
  changes its name: the strip in the week and day grids still reads `all-day`, and so does this
  document, because the word is the clearer one in prose and the button is the one place with no
  room for it.
- three small columns for **stage** — cycles `todo` → `doing` → `done` on each tap, its badge in
  that stage's kanban colour: red, yellow, green. There is no stage popup.
- a `!` for **important** — a straight toggle, lit when the task is important and plain when it
  is not. It carries no badge: a yes or no has nothing a badge could add that the lit state has
  not already said, which is what made the old flag need a digit and this one not.
- an hourglass for **estimate** — the one of the four that opens an editor, because a number has
  to be typed. It opens **inline, beneath the row**, with a trashcan and an `x`, like any other
  field. Its badge reads the day count as `2d`.

On an event, stage, important and estimate are not there at all, because an event has none of
them. They sit here so that a task that is not on a board still carries the two fields a kanban
card edits.

Neither lit control — `24h` or `!` — is the disk's green: in all of Mine green is a save and red
is a trashcan, and a green toggle beside the disk would make the popup look like it offers two
primary actions.

### The details body

Last in the popup, and **shown in full and rendered** — not clipped to two lines, not as raw
markdown — by [Mine's shared renderer](../REQUIREMENTS.md#markdown-bodies). Two lines on a card
and the whole text here are the difference between a glance and having opened the thing, and that
is the one thing the old preview existed for, so it is not spent on making the body look like the
rows above it.

It carries a small header of its own: the `lines` icon, and the trashcan at the right when there
is a body to clear. **Clicking the body makes it active**, replacing the rendered text with the
raw markdown in a textarea and putting the `x` in that same header beside the trashcan. A body
is read far more often than it is written, which is the same argument the rows make, with more
text behind it — and the body's header is the shape every open row takes, since a textarea is
the clearest case for why the buttons do not sit under the editor.

### A new entry

A new entry is **a draft like any other edit**, and no row behaves differently in it. It opens
with its title row active and the when seeded from wherever it was made — the cell, the day
preview's `+`, or a kanban column header, which seeds the stage as well — and every other row is
live from the start. The disk creates the file; until it is pressed, a `+` opened and thought
better of leaves no file and no commit.

**The disk is disabled until the title has something in it**, because an entry must have one.
That is the only way a new entry differs from an edit of a saved one, and it is a disabled button
rather than a rule about which row may be touched first.

### A repeating entry

A repeating entry says so under the title, and carries two things the rest do not:

- **the scope pair**, `this occurrence` or `whole series`, which governs **what the save
  writes**. It is one choice about one write, which is what it always was; it is here rather than
  absent because this popup can write, and the objection it was once kept out of the preview for
  was that a preview could not. Switching it rebuilds the draft from the other file, so it also
  resets what a discard is measured against.
- **`skip this one`**, which drops a single occurrence. That is an action on the entry like
  deleting it, not a change to a field, so it sits with the scope rather than among the rows.

Only the series carries the rule, so **the repetition row is absent on an occurrence override** —
a rule the popup must not rewrite has no row at all.

### Saving, and leaving

The disk **closes the popup and returns to the calendar immediately**; the push to GitHub runs in
the background and is reported in the sync line, not in the popup. **Both ways out land on the
calendar**, the disk and the `x` alike. The cell or the card behind it shows the result anyway,
and there is no preview left to step back to.

I've read the calendar app end to end. Before any implementation, some findings that change the shape of these three asks:

**1. The hamburger already does this — sort of.** `calendar/index.html:103` has `#settings-panel`, a single centred panel titled "Calendar" with a `Filter` section on top and a `Settings` section below. `calendar/REQUIREMENTS.md:617-628` argues explicitly for that merge ("They are one panel because they are one errand… two buttons a thumb's width apart asked which of the two a given switch was before you could reach it"). Your ask reverses that decision. I'll do it, but I want to confirm you mean the reversal and not something smaller (e.g. the sections are there but not legible as two things).

**2. Nothing in the app renders 12-hour time already.** `timeLabel()` in `data.js:137` builds `HH:MM` by hand, the week gutter is `pad(h):00` (`views.js:191`), and the `Intl` formatter is pinned `hour12: false` (`data.js:42`). The one place a locale can still produce AM/PM is the native `<input type="time">` in the when-row — the browser renders that from the OS/browser locale and no attribute or CSS can force it to 24h.

**3. The row-growth problem is real and bigger than `repeat`.** `editorShell()` (`popup.js:370`) deliberately renders an open row as: an uppercase title line with the icon + trashcan + x, then the control on its own line below. So every row goes from 1 line to 2–4 lines on click, and `repeat` goes to 4 (title, "Repeats" + select, "Ends" + 2 controls).

Starting the interview.

content.text:
Design tree is resolved. Here's the agreed spec:

**1. Hamburger → menu of two**
`☰` opens an anchored dropdown with `Filter` and `Settings`. `Filter` opens an anchored dropdown under `☰` (groups unfolded with a scroll cap, plus `important only` + `assignee` on the board only); `Settings` opens the existing centred panel with the filter section removed. Both appear in every view. REQUIREMENTS.md's "one panel because one errand" section gets rewritten to argue the split.

**2. 24h**
The two `<input type="time">` become HH:MM text inputs, normalised on blur (`930`→`09:30`, `9`→`09:00`, `25:00` rejected → reverts). Date inputs stay native. Everything else in the app is already 24h.

**3. Popup rows keep their height**

| row | on click |
|---|---|
| title | inline input, no buttons; closes on Enter / another row / Escape |
| when | anchored popup (4 inputs), row untouched |
| category | anchored popup (group list), row untouched, closes on pick |
| repeat | anchored popup (select + Ends), row untouched |
| alerts / location / participants | inline input, label→placeholder, hints dropped, trashcan + x right-aligned |
| estimate (hourglass) | anchored popup, toggle row untouched |
| details | unchanged |

Row popups are `position: fixed`, layered above the entry popup, no scrim — an outside `pointerdown` closes them and still lands on its target, so switching rows is one tap. Field rows lose the set-before-unset sort and sit in fixed canonical order.

Remaining assumptions, stated rather than asked: Escape cascades (row popup → active row → entry popup); the menu closes when either popup opens; `participants` becomes comma/space-separated on one line.

`test/run.sh` exits 0 — **394 checks, all passing.** All three features are done, with the requirement docs and the test suite in step.

## What changed

**1. Hamburger → two errands** — `☰` opens a two-row dropdown (`filter`, `settings`) and opens neither; a second tap opens the one you meant. `filter` is a dropdown under `☰` with the group checkboxes listed outright (the fold existed only because the settings rows sat below it); `settings` is the centred panel, retitled, with its filter section removed. The board's `important only` and `assignee` stay board-only.

**2. 24-hour, system-wide** — Everything the app renders itself was already `HH:MM`. The only surface that could disagree was the native `<input type="time">` in the when-row, which takes its shape from the device locale and cannot be overridden. Those two are now typed boxes with a parser: `9`→`09:00`, `930`/`0930`→`09:30`, `7:5`→`07:05`; `25:00`, `9:70`, `noon`, `99` are refused and revert. Dates stay native.

**3. Rows hold their shape** — Every row is 52px, open or shut, set or unset, pinned by `min-height` on `.frow` sized to the tallest thing a row can hold. Title/location/alerts/participants become an input in the line (field name as placeholder, trashcan and `x` on that same line); when/category/repeat/estimate open a scrimless popup anchored under the row, leaving the row completely untouched. No scrim means moving between fields is one tap. The set-before-unset sort is gone, so filling a field no longer moves its row either.

## Five things I found and resolved along the way

- The toggle-row taps (all-day, stage, `!`, type pair) silently stopped redrawing once `closeRow` became a no-op on a closed row — added `redraw()`.
- The estimate would have lost its only clear affordance, its row being an icon on the toggle row; its popup head carries the trashcan.
- The title row was missing its `in` class, so its input kept the global 12px padding and grew the row by 26px.
- **Escape narrowed from my stated assumption**: a field popup swallows it, an inline row does not. A new entry opens with its title row already an input, so the full cascade cost two presses to leave the commonest popup in the app.
- One earlier "failure" (`still without writing it`, 2 queued writes) was my own stray headless Chromium squatting on port 9222 from a measurement probe, not the code — it passes clean.

Docs updated to argue the new design rather than the old: `calendar/REQUIREMENTS.md` (the hamburger, the row rules, the when, the filter/settings split), `calendar/TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md` (three overlay mechanisms now, why the third has no scrim, why the anchor is looked up by `data-field`, why a native time input can't be forced), `TEST-REQUIREMENTS.md`, and the README status line. `sw.js` bumped to `2026-11-24.1` so installed apps offer the update.

Name the hamburger's two errands, type the times, and hold a row still

Three changes to the calendar, and the third is the one the other two are
shaped around: a row must not move when it is opened.

The hamburger opens a menu reading `filter` and `settings` and opens
neither. The filter is a dropdown off the button, because the view it
narrows has to stay in sight while it is narrowed, and its groups are
listed rather than folded - that fold existed only because an open list
pushed the nine settings rows below the fold, and the settings are a panel
of their own now.

The when popup's two times are typed `HH:MM` boxes rather than a native
time control, which takes its 12- or 24-hour shape from the device's
locale and cannot be told otherwise. `9` and `900` read back as 09:00,
`930` and `0930` as 09:30, and anything that is not a time of day is
refused. The dates stay native: a picker is worth more than a format, and
a date cannot be misread into a different value. Every time the calendar
renders itself was already 24-hour.

Opening a row no longer changes its height. A row that grew a heading and
a control beneath it moved every row under it, so a popup opened to type
one word rearranged itself and the eye had to find the field again. The
title, location, alerts and participants now hold their input in the line,
with the field's name as the placeholder; the when, category, repetition
and estimate open theirs in a popup anchored to the row, which keeps its
icon, its value and its trashcan. `.frow` carries a min-height set by the
tallest thing a row can hold, so nothing in script equalises anything. The
set-before-unset sort is gone for the same reason it was: filling a field
moved its row.

The field popup carries no scrim, alone among the calendar's overlays. A
scrim would stop the tap that dismisses it, so moving from one field to
the next would take two taps. Escape is swallowed by that popup and not by
an inline row: a new entry opens with its title row already an input, and
